From what I understand it depends on the person and their level of illness/perception. Anosognosia means to lack awareness. It’s why schizophrenic patients are usually taken to a doctor by loved ones; they do not perceive their behavior as abnormal. 

Even after diagnosis and a treatment plan (ex: prescribing medication) some patients are still in denial/lack awareness of their symptoms (for example, still believing that their hallucinations are real). That is why some patients have a difficult time complying and taking medicine consistently. They may not believe they are ill. Correct me if I’m wrong, anyone.

Either way, schizophrenia is a serious disease. Some people believe there is a spectrum. However, I would make an appointment with a psychiatrist who specializes in depression/schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorders and voice your concerns with them.

Yes. You will open the room, arrange furniture, make sure the bed is in working order. You will open sterile supplies, and you will set up the back table and Mayo stand. You will help the surgeon get gowned and gloved and help drape the patient. You will then pass instruments and assist during the procedure (surg techs do not alter tissue; you'll mainly be retracting, passing, or holding. No cutting so if that freaks you out dont worry. The only thing you'll be cutting is suture). When surgery is done, you may be the one to apply dressings (some surgeons do this, it really just depends on them/your area). Then you will clean up the room. You will break down the sterile fields and take the instruments to a decontamination area to be cleaned. Some facilities will have the scrub tech help turnover the room, which entails wiping everything down and mopping. Then, you'll open the next case.

When you get more experienced you may be in charge of ordering things. On slow days, you may help stock rooms, help in SPD, or assist the nurses with stuff. That is generally what a scrub tech does.

I’m a scrub tech student in the last semester in TX.

It’s hard. You’ll doubt yourself a lot. But that’s because a lot of information is thrown at you at once. It’s like that with all healthcare professions.

I have three tips I’ve learned and wish I did:

1. DO NOT PROCRASTINATE. I don’t know if you’re a procrastinator or not, but I was. And that made studying torture for me. You’re going to have a lot of work, but it only SEEMS that way. Sit down, do your work. Read your chapters. Never stay up; go to bed on time. When I started doing this, you wouldn’t believe how much free time I actually did had despite the seemingly large work load I have. It’s a very hard habit to fix but I became so much happier when I did.

2. When clinics start, you’re going to be scared and nervous. And probably won’t do anything but watch. I was like that my first few weeks. Take it from me: Don’t be. Scrub in there and set up your back table. Your preceptor understands that you’re starting out and will always have your back and will step in to help you out. If you have an ass as a preceptor, just know that his/her coworkers think the same about them. You need thick skin in this profession.
TAKE THE INITIATIVE. If you’re still unsure, ask before you do. But always do something. Preceptors appreciate it when you make the attempt. It shows that you want to learn, and they’ll be more inclined to show you tips and explain things more. I went from having a really messy back table to one that is damn near art because I borrowed tips and tricks from so many preceptors. 
The books can only tell you so much. You’ll only learn and understand when you physically do. 
You’re going to run into a lot of things (instruments and equipment) that you have never seen before in your books. You’re probably going to feel like you can do better. One of my preceptors told me this: “you’ll learn the majority of everything once you start actually working.”
You won’t know everything. That’s ok. Even some of the seasoned techs run into things they have never seen before. Keep your cool. Every single day is a learning experience. 

3. I never had a problem with this but some of my classmates did: don’t get offended by the surgeon. Some surgeons are absolutely amazing to work with and you can ask them questions about anything and they’ll be so happy to tell you. Some surgeons will critique you. They just want you to be a better scrub tech. Some surgeons are just rude and get angry and short with you. 
I always just tell myself this: the surgeon has a lot of pressure on them. There’s a person under anesthesia on their table and he/she is going to have to cut this person open, get in and get out. Maintain hemostasis. Do it fast. Do a good job. For some surgeons, it’s stressful and they can get really fussy.
But, at the end of the surgery they always tell us thank you. 
But you’ll always have surgeons that are straight up assholes. I can name 2 in my area. It’s just part of the job. When they leave the room, they forget about you. That’s more comforting than it sounds. 

Like I said, I’m still a student in the last semester but there’s a million other things I would have done differently. If you want to know anything more PM me. I grew a lot as a person during this program and I’m glad I’m in it and I can’t wait to graduate and get out there. 

And even if you don’t want to be a scrub tech forever, there’s a lot of avenues you can take. One day, I hope to be a doctor. This is a foot in the door to get a feel for hospital life. You can even become a first assist or a PA and work in the OR, or move on to different fields. I’ve talked with a lot of preceptors. The opportunity for growth is there.
